Title: That Desk Dizziness Isn't Poor Circulation - It's Your Neck

Description:
Cervicogenic dizziness shows up in roughly 8% of people with neck pain, and over half of patients referred for dizziness and balance issues also report neck and shoulder pain. Your neck's sensory receptors help control balance — when neck muscles tense up or alignment shifts, that signal clashes with what your eyes and ears report, and that mismatch triggers the dizziness. Unlike BPPV's sudden spins, this builds slowly with neck movement or long periods in one position.

Prolonged sitting, forward head posture, and a poorly fitted pillow are common triggers. Keep screens at eye level, take breaks every 30-60 minutes, and pick a pillow that supports your neck's curve.

See a doctor right away if dizziness comes with double vision, slurred speech, or sudden loss of balance.
